Stream3D: Sequential Multi-View 3D Generation
via Evidential Memory

Kaichen Zhou Zeyang Bai Xinhai Chang Affiliation: World Mind Lab, HKUST Affiliation: Media Lab and EECS, MIT    Mengyu Wang Paul Liang Fangneng Zhan Affiliation: Kempner Institute, Harvard University
Abstract

View-conditioned 3D generators such as SAM 3D, TRELLIS and Hunyuan3D produce high-quality object reconstructions from a single view, but real-world visual observation often arrives as long monocular streams. Naively applying these generators to each streaming frame independently leads to severe temporal inconsistency in the generated results. To address this problem, we propose Stream3D, the first training-free streaming mechanism that turns a frozen view-conditioned 3D generator into a streaming generator with constant cross-chunk memory. Stream3D achieves this by maintaining a compact evidential memory, which selectively caches the most informative historical frames based on a proposed evidence score mechanism. As the stream progresses, the memory dynamically updates to retain a fixed number of informative frames, preventing the memory footprint from growing linearly with sequence length. This also prevents degradation over long sequences and keeps the underlying generator completely unchanged without retraining, architectural modifications, or auxiliary losses. Evaluated on both realistic and synthetic streaming benchmarks, Stream3D outperforms latent-transport baselines, including KV-cache reuse and flow-based feature editing, across both photometric and geometric metrics. More details can be found at: Link.

1 Introduction

Object-centric 3D generation is becoming a practical building block for vision and robotics Liu et al. (2023a); Li et al. (2023); Tang et al. (2024). Recent systems such as SAM 3D Objects Chen et al. (2025b) and TRELLIS.2 Xiang et al. (2025a) can take an image, isolate an object, and reconstruct a Gaussian splat Kerbl et al. (2023) or mesh within seconds. Yet their input model remains fundamentally non-streaming. They are designed for a single view, or a small set of views, while real capture devices produce long monocular streams: a phone circling an object, a robot observing while moving, or a wearable camera recording continuously. Naively applying a single-view 3D generator frame by frame yields temporally inconsistent reconstructions; feeding all frames via multi-diffusion method Bar-Tal et al. (2023) or multiview fusion Li et al. (2026) is computationally expensive or even infeasible; and processing fixed-size chunks via a flow matching-based method Kulikov et al. (2025) loses the history needed for global consistency.

An alternative approach is to adapt techniques from streaming video generation or 3D reconstruction Kim et al. (2024); Henschel et al. (2024); Lan et al. (2025); Zhuo et al. (2025). For instance, state-transport mechanisms like KV banks Lan et al. (2025) or FlowEdit-style velocity edits Kulikov et al. (2025) could be introduced to propagate information across chunks. However, transporting latent states in this manner is fundamentally problematic. As the orientation, shape, and scale of these states are deeply entangled within the generator, they are difficult to align across frames, leading to severe error accumulation during the streaming process. Furthermore, as these methods transport and accumulate state over time, their memory footprint naturally grows with sequence length. Ultimately, the transported state itself can become a source of error: over long streams, the very mechanism intended to preserve consistency may paradoxically degrade it.

To solve this problem, we propose Stream3D, a training-free streaming wrapper that turns a frozen view-conditioned 3D generator into a long-stream generator without modifying its weights or architecture. Rather than transporting latent states across chunks, Stream3D retains evidential views: observed frames that the generator itself identifies as reliable conditioning signals through its cross-attention maps. During a lightweight one-step warmup pass, we compute an evidence score for each query token and incoming view, measuring whether the token attends to that view both strongly and selectively. These scores update an Adaptive Evidential Memory, which stores only a fixed number of high-evidence frame indices per query token, keeping memory constant with stream length. At each chunk, token-level evidence is aggregated into frame-level ownership scores, and the top-KK frames are selected as a bounded conditioning bundle for Evidence-Based Multi-Generation. This allows different spatial regions of the 3D volume to retrieve different historical observations, rather than relying on a single global frame subset or an accumulated latent state. As new views arrive, the retained evidence for each query token can only be maintained or improved, yielding a simple non-degradation property in evidence space. In this way, Stream3D avoids latent-space alignment, preserves long-range visual evidence, and enables coherent streaming 3D generation while leaving the original generator unchanged.

We evaluate Streaming3D as a lightweight streaming wrapper around pre-trained SAM 3D on long monocular streams as shown in Fig. 1. Across photometric and geometric metrics, Streaming3D improves over latent-transport baselines while maintaining a constant memory footprint and avoiding the long-horizon degradation observed in KV-bank and FlowEdit-style alternatives. Our contributions are fourfold:

  • •

    Streaming 3D generation. We pioneer the task of extending frozen view-conditioned 3D generators to long monocular streams, producing temporally consistent 3D generations while keeping memory bounded and avoiding retraining.

  • •

    Adaptive Evidential Memory. We introduce a compact memory mechanism that stores token-level evidential views rather than transporting latent states. The memory is interpretable and training-free, with a footprint that remains constant with stream length.

  • •

    Evidence-Based Multi-Generation. We propose an evidence-guided generation strategy that aggregates token-level memory into a bounded conditioning view bundle and runs the frozen generator on the selected views. This enables different spatial regions to draw from the most reliable historical observations without modifying the underlying generator.

  • •

    Superior streaming performance. We show that Stream3D outperforms latent-transport and fixed-view baselines across photometric and geometric metrics, while avoiding long-horizon degradation and maintaining a constant memory footprint.

2 Related Work

2.1 3D Generation

Recent object-centric 3D generators can be understood along three main design axes: output representation, learning regime, and input format. Along the first axis, different methods adopt different 3D representations, including triplane- and Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)-based backbones Hong et al. (2023); Tochilkin et al. (2024); Mildenhall et al. (2020); Yu et al. (2021); Chan et al. (2022); Li et al. (2023); 3DTopia (2023); Wang et al. (2023b), surface meshes Xu et al. (2024a); Wu et al. (2024a); Xiang et al. (2025b); Liu et al. (2023a); Wang et al. (2024b); Wei et al. (2024); Tang et al. (2023b); Gao et al. (2022), 3D Gaussian splats Huang et al. (2025); Kerbl et al. (2023); Tang et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2024b); Tang et al. (2023a); Yi et al. (2024), and native structured latent volumes Zhao et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2024b); Li et al. (2025); Li et al. (2024b); Chen et al. (2025b); Xiang et al. (2025a). Along the second axis, existing approaches cover closed-form regressors Hong et al. (2023); Tochilkin et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2024a); Wu et al. (2024a); Huang et al. (2025); Xiang et al. (2025a); Li et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023a); Tang et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2024b); Wei et al. (2024); 3DTopia (2023); Xu et al. (2024b); Wang et al. (2023b), 3D latent diffusion models Zhao et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2024b); Li et al. (2025); Li et al. (2024b); Chen et al. (2025b); Nichol et al. (2022); Jun and Nichol (2023), and SDS-based optimization methods Poole et al. (2022); Lin et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2023c); Wang et al. (2023a); Metzer et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023); Tang et al. (2023b); Qian et al. (2023); Tang et al. (2023a); Yi et al. (2024); Sun et al. (2023); Qiu et al. (2024). Some layout-aware variants Chen et al. (2025b); Li et al. (2026); Anciukevičius et al. (2023) further model the spatial arrangement of multiple objects within a scene. The third axis, input format, is the one most relevant to our work. Despite their differences in representation and learning paradigm, most existing methods assume a fixed and limited input interface: they take either a single image or a small, predefined set of images as input. Multi-view diffusion methods Liu et al. (2023b); Shi et al. (2023a); Liu et al. (2023c); Long et al. (2024); Shi et al. (2023b); Kong et al. (2024); Voleti et al. (2024); Li et al. (2024a) relax this setting by first hallucinating additional views before reconstructing 3D geometry. Video-conditioned reconstruction models Wang et al. (2024a); Leroy et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025a); Chen et al. (2024b) and 4D-aware generators Bahmani et al. (2024); Singer et al. (2023); Zheng et al. (2023); Zhao et al. (2023); Jiang et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024a); Ren et al. (2024) extend the input format further to short temporal clips. More recently, MV-SAM3D Li et al. (2026) enables multi-view fusion directly in the latent space of a 3D generator. Nevertheless, these methods still operate on a fixed input bundle determined in advance, rather than supporting truly open-ended streaming inputs. None of these methods natively supports unbounded online streams. In practice, long-stream processing is typically handled through ad hoc latent-transport schemes, which propagate intermediate states across chunks. However, such designs usually incur memory growth with sequence length and lead to performance degradation over long horizons. In this work, we adapt a frozen view-conditioned generator Chen et al. (2025b) into a streaming generator that maintains constant cross-chunk memory, independent of stream length, and agnostic to the model backbone.

2.2 Reconstruction from Streaming Inputs

Reconstructing 3D geometry from streaming inputs has traditionally been studied in monocular SLAM Engel et al. (2014); Engel et al. (2018); Davison et al. (2007); Klein and Murray (2007); Newcombe et al. (2011); Forster et al. (2014); Mur-Artal et al. (2015); Mur-Artal and Tardós (2017); Campos et al. (2021); Sun et al. (2021); Matsuki et al. (2024); Huang et al. (2024), which incrementally estimates camera motion and scene structure from video. Recent methods have extended modern feed-forward reconstruction models to online settings. Notably, Spann3R Wang and Agapito (2025) augments a DUSt3R-style encoder Wang et al. (2024a) with a token-addressable spatial memory, enabling online pointmap fusion over long image streams. Similarly, SLAM3R Liu et al. (2025), also built upon DUSt3R, introduces a real-time end-to-end dense reconstruction system that directly predicts 3D pointmaps from RGB videos. Point3R Wu et al. (2025) further incorporates an explicit geometry-aligned spatial pointer memory, together with 3D hierarchical RoPE and an adaptive fusion mechanism. However, DUSt3R itself remains inherently two-view, restricting each inference step to a fixed image pair and making large-scale fusion dependent on iterative matching and optimization. VGGT-SLAM Maggio et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025a) addresses this limitation by adopting the more powerful VGGT transformer, which supports image sets of arbitrary length. CUT3R Wang et al. (2025b) instead adopts an RNN-style formulation for causal pointmap prediction from unstructured image streams. However, it compresses all past observations into a limited recurrent state, which can hinder long-range memorization and fine-grained multi-view fusion. Following the design philosophy of modern large language models, StreamVGGT Zhuo et al. (2025) and Stream3R Lan et al. (2025) employ causal transformers to implicitly cache historical visual tokens. In addition, because CUT3R suffers from severe drift on long streaming inputs, TTT3R Chen et al. (2025a) proposes a simple empirical state-update rule to improve sequence-length generalization. Streaming3D departs from these reconstruction-centered approaches: while online reconstruction focuses on aggregating geometry already observed in the input stream, streaming 3D generation must also infer and synthesize unseen structure under temporal and geometric consistency constraints.

3 Method

We extend view-conditioned 3D generators — SAM 3D Objects Chen et al. (2025b) — to handle long streaming inputs without retraining, architectural change, or auxiliary loss shown in Fig. 2. The Adaptive Evidential Memory (Sec. 3.2) enables efficient long-range memory by retaining token-level evidence from past views, while Evidence-Based Multi-Generation (Sec. 3.3) leverages this memory to produce temporally consistent and geometrically coherent 3D generations throughout the streaming process.

3.1 Problem Setup

3D Generation Preliminary. Let fθf_{\theta} denote a frozen view-conditioned 3D generator that, given a single input frame vv and an initial noise prior z0∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), produces a 3D sample (Gaussian splat Kerbl et al. (2023), mesh, or latent volume) y^=fθ​(v,z0)\hat{y}=f_{\theta}(v;z_{0}). Recent 3D generation models, i.e., SAM 3D Chen et al. (2025b), TRELLIS Xiang et al. (2025b), TRELLIS.2 Xiang et al. (2025a), Hunyuan3D 2.0 Zhao et al. (2025) and CraftsMan3D Li et al. (2024b), instantiate fθf_{\theta} as a two-stage pipeline — a structure stage (SS) producing a coarse occupancy / latent grid, followed by a texture or appearance stage — with at least one cross-attention layer of the form:

𝐀v=softmax⁡(𝐐​𝐊⊤d)∈[0,1]Q×P,\mathbf{A}_{v}\;=\;\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\,\mathbf{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)\;\in\;[0,1]^{Q\times P}, (1)

where QQ is the number of query tokens in the generator’s voxel grid (e.g., 163=409616^{3}=4096 in SAM 3D’s structure stage), PP is the number of key tokens in the input frame vv, and dd is the feature dimension of each query/key token. In its native form, 3D generator fθf_{\theta} accepts a single frame and produces a single reconstruction; it has no mechanism for incorporating multi-view evidence.

Streaming 3D Generation. Our method extends 3D generator fθf_{\theta} to accept a stream of condition views 𝒱={v1,…,vT}\mathcal{V}=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{T}\} by fusing the per-view forward passes through a confidence-weighted Multi-Diffusion-style aggregation in 3D latent space. The stream is partitioned into overlapping chunks 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} of size CC. At chunk kk, we wish to produce a 3D sample y^k\hat{y}_{k} that is consistent with all preceding chunks, while maintaining a memory that does not scale linearly with stream length TT.

3.2 Adaptive Evidential Memory

To maintain an efficient memory footprint that does not scale linearly with the total sequence length TT, we introduce an Adaptive Evidential Memory mechanism shown in Fig. 3. Rather than blindly retaining all historical frames, this approach dynamically filters and preserves only the most informative views by evaluating their relevance at a per-token level. Our mechanism operates in three distinct stages. (1) First, we compute a token-wise Evidence Score via a lightweight attention probe to measure the significance of each incoming view. (2) Second, we update a fixed-capacity global Memory that persistently tracks the highest-scoring frames for each individual query token. (3) Finally, we perform Conditioning-view selection by allowing the tokens to "vote" for their preferred frames, aggregating these local preferences to select an optimal, bounded-size condition set for the full generation pass.

Evidence Score. At a certain chunk, we run a single denoising step of the structure-stage generator on the chunk’s condition set, with a frozen prior z0z_{0} that is sampled once on chunk 00 and reused thereafter. We extract the cross-attention map equation 1 at one fixed layer LL, for a query token qq that excludes special tokens (CLS, register, etc.), and compute the per-token cross-attention induced by view vv (with P patch tokens) as below:

𝐇v[q]=−1log⁡(P)∑i=1P𝐀~v[q,i]log𝐀~v[q,i],𝐀~v[q,i]=𝐀v​[q,i]∑j=1P𝐀v​[q,j],\mathbf{H}_{v}[q]\;=\;-\frac{1}{\log(P)}\sum_{i=1}^{P}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_{v}[q,i]\,\log\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_{v}[q,i],\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_{v}[q,i]=\frac{\mathbf{A}_{v}[q,i]}{\sum_{j=1}^{P}\mathbf{A}_{v}[q,j]}, (2)
𝐌v​[q]=(1+(∑i=1P𝐀v​[q,i]−∑v=1Nc∑i=1P𝐀v​[q,i]Nc))⋅(1−𝐇v​(A~v​[q])),\mathbf{M}_{v}[q]=\left(1+(\sum_{i=1}^{P}\mathbf{A}_{v}[q,i]-\frac{\sum_{v=1}^{N_{c}}\sum_{i=1}^{P}\mathbf{A}_{v}[q,i]}{N_{c}})\right)\cdot\left(1-\mathbf{H}_{v}(\tilde{A}_{v}[q])\right), (3)

which yields a per-view evidence score 𝐌v​[q]∈[0,1]\mathbf{M}_{v}[q]\in[0,1] for query token qq and NcN_{c} is the chunk length. Notably, there are three intentional designs in this probe as explained below: Frozen prior: reusing z0z_{0} across chunks makes evidence score 𝐌v​[q]\mathbf{M}_{v}[q] comparable across chunks; any difference between two chunks’ entropy maps is attributable to the views, not to a fresh draw of noise. Single denoising step: the first step’s attention is dominated by the input views’ content; later steps are progressively shaped by the model’s own prediction, which would be circular for a view-selection objective.

Memory. The cross-chunk memory is represented by two matrices 𝐌,𝐅∈Q×D\mathbf{M},\mathbf{F}\in Q\times D, where QQ is the number of query tokens, and DD is the number of frames to retain, i.e., memory depth. 𝐌∈ℝQ×D\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{Q\times D} is the evidence memory, which stores the DD token-wise highest evidence scores over all observed views; 𝐅∈ℝQ×D\mathbf{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{Q\times D} is the frame-index memory, which stores their corresponding global frame indices. During the streaming process, each token’s top-DD list is updated by merging in the new candidates from newly arriving frames. Frames that never enter any token’s list are discarded immediately. The total footprint is 2×Q×D2\times Q\times D scalars, constant in stream length TT — about 6565 KB for SAM 3D (Q=4096Q{=}4096, D=5D{=}5).

Conditioning-view Selection. At a certain chunk, the runtime view set 𝒱⋆\mathcal{V}^{\star} selected for the full forward pass is obtained by aggregating the per-token top-DD lists into a per-frame token-ownership count, then taking the top-KK frames by that count. Concretely, we define the ownership count of frame frf_{r} as the number of (token, rank) slots it occupies anywhere in 𝐅\mathbf{F}:

nfr=|{(q,j):𝐅[q,j]=fr, 1≤q≤Q, 1≤j≤D}|,n_{f_{r}}\;=\;\big|\{(q,j):\mathbf{F}[q,j]={f_{r}},\ 1\leq q\leq Q,\ 1\leq j\leq D\}\big|, (4)

and select the KK frames with the largest counts for 𝒱⋆\mathcal{V}^{\star}. Notably, there are two distinct ranks DD and KK. DD is the memory depth: how many candidate frames each token retains in its sorted list; KK is the bundle size: how many frames the downstream generator consumes per forward pass. Here, DD controls how robust the evidence score computation is.

3.3 Evidence-Based Multi-Generation

Generation via multi-view flow-matching fusion. The selected views 𝒱⋆\mathcal{V}^{\star} are passed to the generator fθf_{\theta}, which performs multi-view-conditioned diffusion: at each step tt, the generator computes a velocity Vθ​(zt,v)V_{\theta}(z_{t},v) for each v∈𝒱⋆v\in\mathcal{V}^{\star} and fuses the per-view scores into a single update on the shared latent ztz_{t}. Following the standard multi-diffusion fusion rule, the fused velocity at each query token qq is a view-weighted average:

V¯θ​(zt)​[q]=∑v∈𝒱⋆M¯v​[q]​Vθ​(zt,v)​[q],∑v∈𝒱⋆M¯v​[q]=1,\bar{V}_{\theta}(z_{t})[q]\;=\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}^{\star}}\overline{M}_{v}[q]\,V_{\theta}(z_{t},v)[q],\qquad\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}^{\star}}\overline{M}_{v}[q]=1, (5)

where M¯v​[q]\overline{M}_{v}[q] is the normalized per-token, per-view evidence score. The full forward pass is y^=fθ​(𝒱⋆,zk)\hat{y}=f_{\theta}(\mathcal{V}^{\star};z_{k}) with zkz_{k} drawn freely per chunk.

Algorithm and properties. Algorithm 1 summarizes the per-chunk procedure. The method involves three integer hyperparameters (LL, DD, KK), a fixed prior z0z_{0}, and no learned parameters. Processing each chunk requires a single warmup forward pass to extract cross-attention at layer LL, followed by memory updates, and a full forward pass of fθf_{\theta} using the selected conditioning frame bundle.

Summary. The Adaptive Evidential Memory has two structural properties that clearly distinguish it from latent-transport schemes. First, its cross-chunk memory footprint is bounded by at most 2×Q×D2\times Q\times D scalars, and is therefore constant with respect to the stream length TT. Second, for every query token qq and rank jj, the cached evidence score 𝐌⁡[q,j]\mathbf{M}[q,j] is monotonically non-decreasing over time, since each update retains only the top-DD entries from the union of the previous cache and the newly arrived candidates. As a result, the conditioning bundle selected for 3D generation can only stay the same or improve in terms of evidence quality as streaming progresses, while the memory cost remains fixed. By contrast, KV banks and FlowEdit-style velocity edits provide no comparable non-degradation guarantee, and their state typically grows linearly with stream length. Our mechanism simply selects from views that have already been observed, leaves the weights and architecture of fθf_{\theta} unchanged, and requires no additional learning.

4 Experiment

We evaluate Stream3D on long-stream 3D generation, where the model receives a sequence of continuously arriving posed images and must maintain a coherent 3D representation over time. Unlike standard multi-view reconstruction, this setting stresses two properties simultaneously: the method must exploit newly observed views to improve geometry and appearance, while preserving long-range consistency without reprocessing the entire stream. Our experiments are designed to answer three questions: (i) whether Stream3D improves streaming 3D generation quality over single-view and multi-view baselines, (ii) whether token-wise evidential memory provides better long-range consistency than existing streaming alternatives, and (iii) how memory size and view-selection strategy affect performance.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Implementation: Our experiments are run on NVIDIA H100 GPU. We use SAM3D with its standard settings as the underlying generation backbone. We adopt Depth Anything 3 Lin et al. (2025) to estimate the camera pose and depth of initial input to get a point map, which are fed into SAM 3D for 3D generation. We set K=8K=8 and D=1D=1 for efficiency, and provide ablation studies to justify this choice. In all experiments, we evaluate multi-view generation models using streams of length 100.

Dataset: We evaluate on two complementary benchmarks. The first is the GSO benchmark Downs et al. (2022), which contains high-quality scanned objects with ground-truth 3D assets. Following prior multi-view generation and reconstruction protocols, we render posed image streams from each object and evaluate both novel-view appearance and geometric accuracy. This controlled setting allows us to measure whether the generated 3D content remains faithful to the underlying object as the stream length increases. The second benchmark is NAVI Jampani et al. (2023), which provides more complex object-centric view sequences with diverse camera trajectories and challenging viewpoint variation. Compared with GSO, NAVI introduces stronger long-range consistency requirements, since the input stream may contain larger pose changes, partial observations, repeated visual patterns, and more severe self-occlusions.

Baseline: We compare Stream3D with representative single-view, multi-view, and streaming baselines. Single-view baselines, including SAM3D, and TRELLIS, generate 3D content from individual observations and therefore provide a lower bound on streaming consistency. EscherNet serves as a strong multi-view baseline that benefits from multiple posed observations but is not designed for unbounded streaming inputs. We also compare against TRELLIS+M.D. Xiang et al. (2025b) and TRELLIS.2+M.D. Xiang et al. (2025a) which aggregate multiple views through full-context or multi-window diffusion but becomes expensive as the number of frames grows.

Metrics. We report appearance and geometry metrics. For appearance, we use Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) on held-out novel views. These metrics evaluate whether the generated representation renders images that are both photometrically accurate and perceptually faithful. For geometry, we report Patch Fréchet Inception Distance (PFID), Chamfer Distance (CD) and Intersection over Union (IOU). These metrics measure absolute depth quality, relative geometric consistency, and fine-grained 3D accuracy.

4.2 Main Results

Table 1 reports qualitative results on both GSO and NAVI. Fig. 4 shows qualitative results on GSO. Across the two datasets, Stream3D achieves the strongest overall performance on both appearance and geometry metrics. The gains are consistent across all metrics, indicating that the improvement is not limited to image-level rendering quality but also reflects better 3D structure. We could conclude: (1) Compared with single-view baselines such as SAM3D Chen et al. (2025b), TRELLIS Xiang et al. (2025b), and TRELLIS.2 Xiang et al. (2025a), Stream3D substantially improves both appearance and geometry. This confirms that streaming observations provide important information that cannot be recovered from a single image alone. Single-view methods often generate plausible observed geometry but hallucinate unobserved regions inconsistently across time. (2) Compared with multi-view baselines such as TRELLIS+M.D. Xiang et al. (2025b) and TRELLIS.2+M.D. Xiang et al. (2025a), Stream3D shows stronger long-stream behavior. EscherNet benefits from multiple posed views, but it is designed for bounded multi-view input rather than continuously arriving streams. TRELLIS+M.D. can improve consistency by fusing multiple views, but full-context diffusion becomes computationally expensive as the stream grows and does not provide an explicit mechanism for compact long-range memory. Stream3D addresses this limitation by retaining token-level evidence rather than storing or reprocessing all frames. As a result, it maintains high reconstruction quality while keeping memory usage constant.

4.3 Streaming Baseline Comparison

Table 2 further compares Stream3D with several streaming alternatives. Fig. 5 report qualitative results. (1) We compare against MV-SAM3D-style Li et al. (2026) fixed-view selection to evaluate whether a small set of representative views can serve as an effective substitute for streaming memory. Random view sampling is unstable, as it may discard observations that are critical for reconstructing specific geometric regions. More broadly, these results reveal the limitation of frame-level view selection: streaming generation requires a finer-grained memory mechanism, since different spatial tokens may rely on evidence from different historical views. A frame that is highly informative for one surface region can be irrelevant, redundant, or even misleading for another. In contrast, Stream3D maintains token-level evidential memory, enabling each spatial region to retrieve the historical observations that best support its generation. (2) We also compare against cache- and transport-based streaming baselines. KV-cache reuse provides an efficient mechanism for carrying historical information forward, but cached tokens are not explicitly filtered according to geometric reliability. As a result, the memory can accumulate stale or ambiguous evidence, especially under long camera motion. FlowEdit performs local flow-based latent editing and improves short-range consistency, but it operates on fixed-size chunks and therefore loses long-range history. This limitation becomes visible in long streams, where global consistency depends on observations that may fall outside the current editing window. In contrast, Stream3D maintains a compact but persistent evidence memory. The memory does not simply reuse all past latent states; it selects and aggregates historical information according to token-level evidence. (3) We also compare Stream3D with MV-SAM3D Li et al. (2026), which selects a compact set of informative input views using visibility-aware weighting. Although MV-SAM3D is effective in bounded multi-view settings, it is not designed for streaming generation: once the input stream grows, selecting a small global view subset can discard historical observations that are locally important for specific surfaces or tokens. In contrast, Stream3D maintains a token-wise evidential memory, allowing different spatial regions to retrieve different historical views according to their accumulated evidence. This provides a more flexible and scalable mechanism for long-stream generation, preserving global consistency without requiring all past frames to be regenerated or jointly fused.

4.4 Ablation Studies

We conduct detailed ablation studies in Tab. 3 to analyze the influence of different evidence scoring and view selection strategies on both geometric consistency and visual quality.

First, we investigate the effect of the stage used for evidence computation. Following Chen et al. (2025b), we denote the first generation stage as SS and the second generation stage as SLAT. Comparing different stage combinations, such as SS6-SLAT3, SS6-SLAT6, SS9-SLAT3, SS9-SLAT6, and SS9-SLAT9, we observe that deeper stages consistently provide better geometry-aware evidence estimation. In particular, SS becomes stable after stage 9, while SLAT becomes stable after stage 6. Using SS9-SLAT6 achieves substantially lower CD-L2 and better α\alpha-IoU than shallow-stage configurations, while also improving appearance metrics including PSNR and LPIPS. This suggests that deeper transformer features encode more reliable multi-view geometric correspondence for streaming view selection.

Next, we compare different evidence normalization strategies. Besides our proposed normalized Evidence weighting, we evaluate entropy-based scoring (ENT) and an unnormalized variant Evidence(N). Results show that normalized Evidence consistently outperforms both alternatives across geometry and appearance metrics. ENT leads to weaker geometric alignment, while Evidence(N) suffers from degraded stability and higher perceptual errors. These results indicate that proper normalization is critical for balancing confidence across candidate views and preventing dominance.

We further study the effect of memory depth MM. Compared with M=1M=1, increasing the memory depth to M=3M=3 and M=5M=5 improves both geometry and appearance metrics, indicating that retaining multiple high-evidence historical views is beneficial for long-range consistency. However, further increasing the memory depth to M=7M=7 does not consistently improve all metrics: while it can slightly improve some appearance scores, it may also introduce weaker or stale evidence from less reliable historical frames. Overall, M=3M=3 achieves the best P-FID, while M=5M=5 offers a strong and stable trade-off across geometry, appearance, and memory cost.

Finally, we analyze the influence of TopK view selection. Using too few views (K=4K=4) significantly degrades both geometry and appearance quality due to insufficient multi-view coverage. Increasing the number of selected views from K=8K=8 to K=16K=16 only brings moderate changes in performance, suggesting that the method is relatively stable once enough informative views are included. In particular, K=16K=16 achieves the best overall results on most metrics, including CD-L2, α\alpha-IoU, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and Img-FID, demonstrating that richer multi-view aggregation can further improve geometric reconstruction and visual consistency, although the gain over K=8K=8 is not large.

5 Limitations

The method is built on top of the quality of the underlying pretrained generator. If the base model fails to reconstruct the object from individual views, the proposed evidential memory cannot fully recover the missing geometry or appearance.

6 Conclusion

We introduced Stream3D, a training-free framework that extends frozen view-conditioned 3D generators to long monocular streams. Instead of transporting latent states across chunks, Stream3D uses the generator’s cross-attention maps to identify historical views that provide reliable conditioning evidence for each 3D query token. This evidence is stored in a compact Adaptive Evidential Memory and used by Evidence-Based Multi-Generation to select a bounded view bundle for each chunk. As a result, Stream3D keeps memory constant with stream length while leaving the original generator unchanged. Experiments on GSO and NAVI show that Stream3D improves both appearance and geometry over single-view generators, multi-view diffusion baselines, and streaming alternatives such as KV-cache reuse and flow-based feature editing. These results support our central claim: streaming 3D generation is better addressed as an evidence selection problem than as a latent transport problem. By preserving token-level evidential views rather than unstable latent states, Stream3D provides a scalable path toward coherent long-horizon 3D generation from continuously arriving visual observations.
